clue.text: Bottle we turned up on this day in 1924?

parts.note: someone born on this date in 1924 turned 100 on the day the puzzle appeared (9 August 2024); C is the Roman numeral for 100
if we had turned up, been born, then, that hundred would be our age

explanation.surface: Someone recalls bravely producing a bottle on a particular centenary date.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as 'C, our age': for anyone who turned up (was born) on this day in 1924, their age on publication day is C, 100. DUTCH COURAGE is one of the puzzle's themed phrases.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottle is British slang for nerve or bravery, as in 'to lose your bottle'.

clue.text: Bed welcoming maiden for relief

indicators.note: welcoming a guest means taking them in, so the bed holds the following letters

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bed that takes in a young woman as an act of kindness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like the link word but is part of the wordplay. DUTCH COMFORT is the themed phrase: 'it could have been worse'.
explanation.definitionFit: Comfort is relief from pain or distress, the easing of a burden.

clue.text: Fully informed American went to take look on other side

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: US is short for American
PTO, please turn over, tells a reader to look on the other side of the page
went is a euphemism for urinated

explanation.surface: A well-briefed American checks the reverse of a document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went' is used in the euphemistic sense of going to the loo, and PTO is the note printed at the foot of a page.
explanation.definitionFit: To be up to speed is an idiom for being fully briefed on the latest developments.

clue.text: Increasingly on the ball, but for Beckenbauer holding line

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: aber is German for but; Franz Beckenbauer is a German footballer
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A footballer, the great German defender Beckenbauer, getting sharper as he holds the defensive line.
explanation.walkthrough: Beckenbauer is there to signal German: but in German is aber. 'On the ball' fits the football surface but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: On the ball means alert and competent; increasingly so is abler, the comparative of able.

clue.text: What brings the curtain down on the Daisy Festival

indicators.text: What brings the curtain down on
indicators.note: bringing the curtain down ends a show, so the final letter of the next word is wanted

parts.note: the last letter of this word
the aster is a daisy-like flower of the same family

explanation.surface: A question about the finale of a flower show.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'the' is the word whose ending is taken. Asters belong to the daisy family; a Michaelmas daisy is an aster.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter is the Christian festival of the Resurrection held in spring.

clue.text: Controls reversible as draught screens

indicators.note: something reversible can be turned the other way round, so the concealed letters are read from right to left
to screen something is to conceal it, so the answer lies concealed inside the following words

parts.note: the letters of this phrase, read backwards, run through a six-letter word

explanation.surface: A householder buys draught excluders that can be flipped to use either side.
explanation.walkthrough: Written backwards, 'as draught' is THGUARDSA; the answer sits in the middle. 'Screens' looks like the noun the clue is about but is the signal to look inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To guard your tongue or temper is to control it, so guards works as a verb meaning restrains or controls.

clue.text: To close dodgy deal on counter, sell fine sheets

indicators.note: counter means running in the opposite direction, so the word is read backwards
to close round something is to shut it in, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: flog is British slang for sell

indicators.note: something dodgy is crooked, so the letters are bent into another order

parts.note: the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A trader closes a shady deal over the shop counter, selling fine linen.
explanation.walkthrough: FLOG turned round is GOLF, which wraps the rearranged letters of deal. 'Counter' looks like a shop counter but signals the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold leaf is gold beaten into extremely thin sheets for gilding.

clue.text: Rolled leather antique given royal provision

indicators.note: something rolled is turned over, so the word for leather is read the other way round

parts.note: nappa is soft leather made from sheepskin or kid
an antique is old, or aged

explanation.surface: A rolled-up leather antique handed over as a gift from royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: An appanage is land or revenue granted to a younger royal child for support, so appanaged means endowed with one.

clue.text: 'Arry's other 'alf — or perhaps 'alves!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Cockney 'my old ...' is one's wife, a man's other half
second meaning: going ... is splitting the bill in halves

explanation.walkthrough: The dropped aitches signal Cockney speech, where 'my old Dutch' means my wife. The puzzle is a tribute to the late Toughie blogger Dutch.
explanation.definitionFit: Dutch is Cockney slang for a wife, and going Dutch means each paying their own half of the bill.

clue.text: Rural worker dispatched vegetables

indicators.note: dispatched means sent away or killed off, so that part is removed

parts.note: peasant as an adjective means rustic or rural
the worker ant is the crossword's usual worker

explanation.surface: A farmhand who was sent off to deal with the vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rural worker' wants to be one thing, a farm labourer; it is two, with the worker removed from the rural word.
explanation.definitionFit: Peas are green vegetables, the seeds of a climbing legume eaten fresh or dried.

clue.text: Satisfied element 13 constitutes this?

parts.note: a demand that is met has been satisfied
element 13 in the periodic table is aluminium, chemical symbol Al

explanation.surface: A chemist is pleased to find that aluminium makes up the sample.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: aluminium, element 13, is itself a metal. DUTCH METAL is an imitation gold leaf made of brass.
explanation.definitionFit: Aluminium is a classic example of a metal, so the question asks what category element 13 belongs to.

clue.text: Pestle and mortar only half ground white powder

indicators.note: something ground is crushed and broken up, so the letters are mixed into a new order
only half of the word is kept, the other half being thrown away

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then cut to its back half

explanation.surface: A chemistry recipe: grind the powder in a pestle and mortar, but only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second half of mortar, TAR, joins PESTLE before the letters are rearranged. The surface's 'ground' is the grinding you do in a pestle and mortar.
explanation.definitionFit: Saltpetre, potassium nitrate, is a white crystalline powder used in gunpowder and food curing.

clue.text: Are spectators missing Wimbledon's Centre Court shots?

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so that letter is taken out of the shot
the centre of a word is its middle letter, which is the one taken

parts.note: the fifth of the nine letters is the centre one
two tennis shots: a lob, lofted over the opponent, and a serve

explanation.surface: A question about whether crowds are missing out on play at Centre Court, Wimbledon's main show court.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon's Centre Court is the famous arena, but here 'Wimbledon's Centre' is a single letter and 'Court shots' are the two strokes, the first losing that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectators watch, so to be spectators is to observe; the plural verb matches 'are'.

clue.text: Free ones supply endless cheerfulness!

definitions.note: with 'Free' in front, the clue names FREE LUNCHES

indicators.note: supply is read as the adverb 'supply', pliantly, so the letters bend into another order
without an end means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: taken as written: these letters plus the answer form the anagram
with its final letter removed

explanation.surface: Free things handed out make everybody endlessly cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: A compound anagram: FREE plus the answer, rearranged, gives CHEERFULNES. Take FREE out of those letters and the rest form the answer. 'Ones' stands for the answer, so 'Free ones' is FREE LUNCHES.
explanation.definitionFit: A free lunch is something got for nothing, and 'ones' stands in for the plural noun so 'Free ones' means free lunches.

clue.text: Risks bypassing hospital doctors

indicators.note: to bypass a place is to go round it without stopping, so that letter is left out

parts.note: threats are dangers or risks
H is the map and road-sign abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: Risky medics who avoid going through a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctors' looks like a plural noun but is the verb: a doctor treats a patient. DUTCH TREAT is the themed phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor treats patients, giving them medical care, so doctors and treats are matching verbs.

clue.text: With frivolity, constantly one goes on bottle rather than head to university

indicators.note: putting one thing rather than another means swapping it in where the other was

parts.note: constant means faithful, and so does true; constantly is truly
I is the Roman numeral one
a vial is a small bottle

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, which is the one kept

parts.note: the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: A person who drinks frivolously instead of going to university.
explanation.walkthrough: In TRULY, the U is replaced by I and VIAL together; 'goes on' just joins one to bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivially means in a trifling, unserious way, which is how something done with frivolity is done.

clue.text: A good deal, but for profit

parts.note: but and bar both mean except, as in 'all but one' or 'all bar one'
a gain is a profit

explanation.surface: Someone reflects that a deal was good, but only for making money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But' looks like the conjunction; it is the preposition meaning except. A DUTCH BARGAIN is one struck over drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargain is a purchase made cheaply, a good deal for the buyer.

clue.text: Sit with Renoir for exciting pictures

indicators.note: exciting means stirring up, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Posing for the painter Renoir to make thrilling paintings.
explanation.walkthrough: Renoir points to French Impressionism, but the theme is Dutch: Dutch interiors are domestic scenes by painters like Vermeer.
explanation.definitionFit: Interiors are paintings of indoor domestic scenes, a genre the Dutch masters were famous for.

clue.text: Gilded French Noble dropping ring? It shouldn't be missed

indicators.note: dropping something lets it fall, and in a down entry that letter falls lower, leaving its place for a later one

parts.note: in French word order a gilded baron is baron d'or, the adjective coming after
a ring is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: A golden French aristocrat who has lost a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: In the down light the first O of BARON D'OR falls two places, giving BARN DOOR. The definition alludes to the saying that someone couldn't hit a barn door.
explanation.definitionFit: A barn door is proverbially so large a target that anyone should hit it, so it shouldn't be missed.

clue.text: I am a lord at sea, taking over

definitions.text: I am a lord at sea, taking over

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are reordered
taking a letter means taking it away, so the round letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A naval commander announces his rank as he assumes command of the fleet.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a senior naval officer is a lord at sea who takes over command. A DUTCH ADMIRAL fits the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: An admiral is a commander of a fleet, often styled a Lord of the Admiralty, so a lord at sea.

clue.text: One of our bosses who didn't see low beam, we 'ear?

indicators.note: we hear, said in Cockney with a dropped H, means what follows is judged by sound

parts.note: someone who missed a low beam hit their head: a head-hitter, said with dropped aitches

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor who walked into a low beam, as overheard in a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the aitches, as the apostrophe in 'ear signals, 'head-hitter' comes out as 'ead 'itter. The editor is the boss of a newspaper's crossword setters.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's editor is in charge of setters and bloggers alike, so is one of their bosses.

clue.text: New beer brewers finally accepting UK rates

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so these letters go inside
a new version is made over, so the letters take a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so the last letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the final letter of this word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Brewers of a new beer accept British tax rates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rates' looks like a noun, as in tax rates, but is the verb meaning scolds.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate someone is an old sense meaning to scold them angrily, as does rebukes.

clue.text: Moral code keeps knight out of the race

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the code holds the next piece inside

parts.note: an ethic is a set of moral principles
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A code of honour that bars a knight from competing in a tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: The race is a people, not a contest; 'out of' is read as 'from', springing from a people.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethnic means relating to a people sharing a common origin or culture, a race in the older sense.

clue.text: Lawsuit restricts United sale

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so one word holds the other inside it

parts.note: an action is a legal case brought in court
U is the abbreviation for United in football club names

explanation.surface: A court case blocks a football club's sale.
explanation.walkthrough: A DUTCH AUCTION starts high and the price falls until someone bids.
explanation.definitionFit: An auction is a public sale in which goods go to the highest bidder.

clue.text: Too involved in choral society…

indicators.note: being involved in something means being caught up within it, so the answer is inside the words

parts.note: runs across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone also joining a choir, the sentence running on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue to the next in the surface reading only; each is solved alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Too and also are synonyms, both meaning in addition.

clue.text: …conduct hymn?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to run a meeting as its presiding officer
second meaning, cryptically: a church air, CH being the abbreviation for church

explanation.walkthrough: Read with the previous clue, it pictures someone conducting a choir. The question mark flags that the second meaning is split: CH for church plus AIR for a tune.
explanation.definitionFit: To chair a meeting is to conduct it, and a hymn is a church song, a church air.

clue.text: One regrets infiltrating little back part of the cage

indicators.note: to infiltrate is to get inside, so one piece slips into the other
going back means reading from right to left, so the small word is turned round

parts.note: a bit is a little
one who rues, or regrets, is a ruer

explanation.surface: A remorseful spy sneaks a short way into a cage.
explanation.walkthrough: The cage is the ribcage, not one for an animal; the little word is turned round before it wraps the regretter.
explanation.definitionFit: True ribs are the upper seven pairs attached directly to the breastbone, making up part of the ribcage.

clue.text: This member of the family is versatile in clues

indicators.note: something versatile can take many forms, so the letters can be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters that join the answer in the anagram

explanation.surface: A family member who is good at solving crossword clues.
explanation.walkthrough: A compound anagram: the answer plus IS can be rearranged as IN CLUES; remove IS from those letters and the rest form the answer. A DUTCH UNCLE gives stern advice.
explanation.definitionFit: An uncle is a parent's brother, a member of one's family.

clue.text: Provincial shops store any number of bags

indicators.note: to bag something is to take it in, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: to stow is to store away
a mall is a covered collection of shops
n stands for any number in algebra

explanation.surface: Country shops keep a stock of all kinds of bags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' looks like the goods on sale, but it is the verb meaning captures.
explanation.definitionFit: Small-town describes the narrow, parochial outlook associated with the provinces rather than the capital.

clue.text: 11 what's down on face
Look to enter a petition

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one word slips inside the other

parts.note: a, as in 'ten pounds a head', means per
a ray is a beam, as a look or glance can be thought of

explanation.surface: An instruction to read a petition before signing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' is not just the article: it means 'each', as in a price of ten pounds a head.
explanation.definitionFit: A prayer is a petition or earnest request, especially one addressed to God.

clue.text: Charlie Guy's experience winding through Swaledale and Wensleydale?

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: going through something means passing inside it, so these letters sit within the other word

parts.note: a guy is a he, so guy's becomes he's

indicators.note: winding means twisting about, so the letters are turned into a new order

parts.note: to see something is to experience it

explanation.surface: A man called Charlie tells of hiking through two of the Yorkshire Dales.
explanation.walkthrough: Swaledale and Wensleydale are valleys in the Yorkshire Dales, but also cheeses named after them; the question mark flags the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Wensleydale and Swaledale are both hard cheeses made in the Yorkshire valleys whose names they carry.
